extracted.intended_audience: general public; researchers; journalists interested in American Family Association and related controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article summarizing the American Family Association's positions, controversies, criticisms, and external reactions over time. Presents quoted statements, third-party responses, legal and advocacy-group actions, and sourced references.

rubrics_metrics.name: CyberPatrol 'intolerance' classification
rubrics_metrics.description: CyberPatrol blocked the AFA's web site, classifying it under the category 'intolerance', defined as 'pictures or text advocating prejudice or discrimination against any race, color, national origin, religion, disability or handicap, gender or sexual orientation...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sites that publish content advocating prejudice or discrimination (examples cited: quotes warning that neutrality toward homosexual rights will 'result in society's destruction'; calls to 'outlaw public homosexuality'; claims that homosexuality 'leads ultimately to personal and social decay') meet CyberPatrol's intolerance criteria and may be blocked by content-control tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'language of violence and hatred' in advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious Leadership Roundtable criticized AFA-sponsored full-page newspaper advertisements as employing 'language of violence and hatred to denounce other people'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisements that denounce groups or individuals using violent or hateful language are flagged by religious leaders and community groups as unacceptable; such language is used as a basis for public condemnation and mobilization against the advertiser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard for the 'dignity of every human being' (Christian ethical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: IntegrityUSA criticized the AFA advertisements as 'evil,' saying they disregard Christian teachings about the 'dignity of every human being'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith-based critics apply a standard that religious messaging should respect human dignity; messaging judged to contravene that standard is condemned within religious-ethical discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising judged 'misleading and destructive'
rubrics_metrics.description: DignityUSA labelled the AFA advertisements as 'misleading and destructive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocacy or religious advertisements that are perceived as factually misleading or socially destructive may be singled out by community organizations and used as grounds for public rebuttal, protests, or calls for accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions that 'constitute and encourage violence' toward LGBTQ people
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality Mississippi noted that AFA's actions were 'constituting and encouraging violence toward the LGBTQ community'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil-rights groups treat organizational activities or rhetoric that they view as encouraging violence as actionable harms—these assessments can prompt calls for investigations, public pressure, or legal responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized use of copyrighted images in campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2005 Equality Mississippi publicly spoke out against the AFA for using copyrighted images on its website without permission as part of a boycott campaign against Kraft Foods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using copyrighted material without permission exposes organizations to legal risk and public criticism; affected parties and allies may be encouraged to file suit and seek remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering news agency copy / editorial manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: AFA's OneNewsNow replaced instances of 'gay' with 'homosexual' in re-posted AP articles and altered athletes' names (e.g., rendering 'Tyson Gay' as 'Tyson Homosexual').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering wire-service copy or individuals' names to fit an agenda is treated as a breach of journalistic integrity and is highlighted by media-watch organizations as an anti-pattern; it provokes public embarrassment and criticism from journalistic and advocacy communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging in 'hate speech'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) said in a 2005 report that the AFA engaged in 'hate speech' that 'help[ed] drive the religious right's anti-gay crusade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of demeaning, demonizing, or dehumanizing language about a protected group is characterized as hate speech by civil-rights organizations and is used as evidence in policy reports and public listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation of known falsehoods and 'demonizing propaganda' (basis for hate-group designation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark Potok of the SPLC identified the AFA's 'propagation of known falsehoods and demonizing propaganda' as the basis for changing its listing from a group that used hate speech to a formal 'hate group' designation in November 2010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated dissemination of demonstrably false claims and systematic demonization of a protected group can form the basis for an organization being designated a hate group by monitoring organizations; such a designation carries reputational consequences and prompts organized responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal accountability for rhetoric that fosters discrimination and violence
rubrics_metrics.description: San Francisco's Board of Supervisors (led by Leslie Katz) wrote that rhetoric denouncing gays and lesbians contributes to a climate of mistrust and discrimination that can open the door to 'horrible crimes' (citing Matthew Shepard and other incidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local government bodies may adopt resolutions calling for accountability from rhetoric-producing groups, asserting that public speech that denounces protected groups has real-world harms and should be publicly condemned or countered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational disciplinary/ reputational consequences for extreme public statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The article records widespread criticism of Bryan Fischer's statements (e.g., blaming homosexuals for the Holocaust), reporting that AFA later fired Fischer and that various groups repudiated his remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme, racist, or demeaning public statements by prominent organizational spokespeople can lead to internal disciplinary action (including termination), external denunciation, loss of partnerships, and broader reputational harm; organizations are therefore judged by how they respond to such statements.
